usage: Standard polite question to any shopkeeper
반말, only to a friend or younger seller you know
Formal 합쇼체, stiff but very polite
Asking the total for several items
examples: 이거 얼마예요?
How much is this?
Bare question while pointing at one item
사장님, 이 사과 한 봉지에 얼마예요?
Boss, how much for a bag of these apples?
사장님 is the polite way to address any shop owner
저기요, 이 가방 색깔별로 가격이 달라요? 검은색은 얼마예요?
Excuse me, are the prices different by color? How much is the black one?
저기요 gets attention first; 색깔별로 = by color
nuance: 얼마예요? is the single most useful shopping phrase, said by a customer to a seller to ask a price; 얼마 means 'how much/how many' and 예요 is the polite copula, so it literally asks 'it is how much?'. The politeness sits at the everyday 해요체 level — perfectly polite for markets, shops and taxis — and you drop to 얼마야? only with a friend, or rise to 얼마입니까? in a formal counter or on the phone. The nearest alternative, 가격이 어떻게 돼요? ('what's the price?'), is a touch softer and more common for services or quotes, while 얼마예요? is the blunt, direct market question; the dividing line is that 얼마예요? names a number you expect right now. The classic English-speaker mistake is writing 얼마에요 — the copula after a vowel is 예요, not 에요 — and saying 얼마이에요, which is over-spelled; native spelling is 얼마예요.

mistakes: Spelling it 얼마에요.
After a noun ending in a vowel the polite copula is -예요, not -에요. The correct, natural spelling is 얼마예요?
Asking 얼마 많아요? thinking 많다 means 'much'.
많다 is 'many/a lot' (quantity), not price. Price uses the fixed word 얼마, so it is 얼마예요?
Using 얼마야? with a shop clerk you don't know.
얼마야? is 반말 and sounds rude to a stranger. To any seller use 얼마예요? or 얼마입니까?

usage: Pointing at one item near you, polite
반말 to a friend running a stall
Formal 합쇼체, 이것은 is the full written form
저거 = that thing over there, out of reach
examples: 이거 얼마예요?
How much is this?
Touching or pointing at the item as you ask
이거 얼마예요? 두 개 사면 좀 싸게 해 주세요.
How much is this? If I buy two, give me a little discount.
Bundling for a deal; 싸게 = cheaply
이거 얼마예요? 아, 생각보다 비싸네요. 좀 더 둘러볼게요.
How much is this? Oh, pricier than I thought. I'll look around a bit more.
Polite exit after hearing the price; 생각보다 = than expected
nuance: 이거 얼마예요? is the pointing version of the price question, said by a customer holding or gesturing at one specific item right in front of them; 이거 is the spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing'), so it means 'this — how much?'. It stays at polite 해요체, the default for shops; with a friend's stall you can say 이거 얼마야?, and in a formal showroom 이것은 얼마입니까?. The key three-way distance system is 이거 (this, near me) / 그거 (that, near you) / 저거 (that, far from both), and English speakers, who only have 'this/that', constantly mix up 그거 and 저거. The nearest alternative is just 얼마예요? with a point, but adding 이거 removes all ambiguity about which item — useful when several sit side by side. The typical mistake is saying 이것 얼마예요? in speech: in conversation Koreans almost always shorten 이것 to 이거, and they attach no particle (not 이거가/이거를) before 얼마예요.

mistakes: Saying 이것 얼마예요? in conversation.
이것 is the written form; spoken Korean contracts it to 이거. Natural speech is 이거 얼마예요?
Adding a particle: 이거를 얼마예요?
얼마예요 takes no object; the thing is simply named as the topic. Say 이거 얼마예요? with no 를/가.
Using 저거 for an item right in your hand.
저거 means 'that, far away'. For something you're holding use 이거. Pick the right distance word.

usage: Please knock the price down a bit
반말 to a friend or familiar vendor
Couldn't you take just a little off?
If you take some off, I'll buy right away
Offering to close the deal as leverage
examples: 좀 깎아 주세요.
Please give me a discount.
Bare haggle line at a traditional market stall
두 개 살게요. 좀 깎아 주세요.
I'll take two. Give me a bit of a discount, please.
Volume as a bargaining chip; common market move
현금으로 낼게요. 만 원만 깎아 주세요.
I'll pay cash. Take off just 10,000 won, please.
Cash offer for a discount; 만 원만 = just 10,000 won
nuance: 좀 깎아 주세요 is a customer's haggling request at a place where bargaining is normal — traditional markets (시장), street stalls, some electronics alleys — but NOT department stores, franchises or convenience stores, where it falls flat. 깎다 literally means 'to shave/whittle down', so you ask the seller to 'shave a bit off (the price)'; 좀 ('a little') is the softener that makes it polite rather than pushy, and 주세요 makes it a request 'for me'. It sits at polite 해요체; drop to 깎아 줘 only with a friend, and soften upward with 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? ('couldn't you take some off?'). The nearest alternative, 싸게 해 주세요 ('make it cheap for me'), asks for a lower price in general, while 깎아 주세요 specifically asks to reduce THIS quoted number — the dividing line is that 깎다 acts on an already-stated price. English speakers translate 'discount' as the loanword 디스카운트 or say 할인해 주세요 (할인 is the store's own 'sale', odd to demand by hand), which sounds unnatural at a market; the native haggle is 깎아 주세요.

Dropping 좀 and just saying 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without 좀 it sounds blunt, almost like an order. 좀 softens it into a polite request, so include it.
Trying to haggle in a department store or chain.
깎아 주세요 only works where bargaining is expected (markets, stalls). In fixed-price shops it just confuses the clerk.

usage: Polite reaction to a high price
반말 muttered to a companion or friend
Softer, indirect — gentler than a flat 비싸요
examples: 너무 비싸요.
It's too expensive.
Bare reaction right after hearing the price
우와, 너무 비싸요. 좀 깎아 주세요.
Wow, that's too expensive. Give me a discount, please.
Pairing the complaint with a haggle request
디자인은 마음에 드는데 너무 비싸요. 좀 더 생각해 볼게요.
I like the design, but it's too expensive. I'll think about it more.
Polite soft no; -는데 sets up the 'but'
nuance: 너무 비싸요 is what a customer says reacting to a price they find too high, to a seller or to a friend beside them; 비싸다 means 'to be expensive' and 너무 means 'too (much)', so it is 'it's too expensive'. Said directly to a seller it doubles as the opening move of haggling, especially at markets. It is polite 해요체; with friends it's 너무 비싸, and to sound gentler — so you don't seem to insult the goods — Koreans soften to 좀 비싼 것 같아요 ('it seems a bit pricey'), which is the more tactful register shift. The nearest pair is 비싸다 (expensive) vs 싸다 (cheap); do not confuse 싸다 with 사다 ('to buy') — same Romanization 'sada' but different verbs. A frequent English-speaker error is using 너무 as a plain intensifier like 'very' in praise; classically 너무 carries a negative 'excessively' edge, so 너무 비싸요 fits, but for 'very good' careful speakers prefer 정말/아주 좋아요. Also note 너무 비싸요, not 너무 비싸여요 — 비싸다 is already 비싸 + 요.

They are opposites. 비싸다 = expensive, 싸다 = cheap. Saying 너무 싸요 means 'it's too cheap', the reverse complaint.
Writing 너무 비싸여요.
비싸다's polite form is 비싸 + 요 = 비싸요, no extra 여. The correct form is 너무 비싸요.
Mixing up 싸다 (cheap) and 사다 (buy).
Different verbs that romanize alike. 싸다 = be cheap, 사다 = to buy. Context and spelling keep them apart.

usage: Polite request to a clothing clerk
반말 to a friend shopping with you
Would it be okay to try it on?
Stating intent after getting the okay
examples: 이거 입어 봐도 돼요?
Can I try this on?
Bare request while holding a garment
이 셔츠 입어 봐도 돼요? 탈의실 어디예요?
Can I try this shirt on? Where's the fitting room?
Natural follow-up; 탈의실 = fitting room
사이즈가 애매해서요, 입어 봐도 돼요? M이랑 L 둘 다 볼게요.
The size is borderline, so can I try it on? I'll check both M and L.
Real situation; 애매하다 = borderline/unclear
nuance: 입어 봐도 돼요? is a customer asking a clothing clerk for permission to try a garment on; it is built from 입다 ('to wear/put on') + the -아/어 보다 'try doing' pattern + -아도 돼요? 'is it okay to...?', so literally 'is it okay if I try wearing it?'. The crucial point is that Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 for clothes on the torso/legs (shirts, pants, dresses), 신다 for shoes/socks on the feet, 쓰다 for hats/glasses, 끼다 for gloves/rings — so this exact phrase is only for clothes you 입다. It is polite 해요체; soften to 입어 봐도 될까요? for extra deference, or 입어 봐도 돼? with a friend. The nearest alternative, 한번 봐도 돼요? ('can I take a look?'), only asks to look, not to put on — 입어 봐도 돼요? specifically asks to wear it. English speakers literally translate 'try on' and may say 시도해 봐도 돼요? (시도 = 'attempt', wrong here) or use 입어 for shoes; both miss. Use 입어 for tops, 신어 for shoes.

입다 is for clothing on the body, not feet. Shoes take 신다, so for shoes ask 신어 봐도 돼요?

시도하다 means 'to attempt' (an action), not to try clothing. The fitting-room verb is 입어 보다: 입어 봐도 돼요?
Writing 입어 봐도 되요?
The polite form of 되다 here is 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요. Correct: 입어 봐도 돼요?

usage: Polite request in a shoe shop
Would it be okay to try them on?
한 사이즈 큰 거 신어 볼게요
Asking to test the next size
examples: 이거 신어 봐도 돼요?
Can I try these on?
Bare request pointing at a shoe on display
이 운동화 신어 봐도 돼요? 250 사이즈로요.
Can I try these sneakers on? In size 250.
Korean shoe sizes are in mm; 250 = 25.0 cm
발이 좀 넓어서요, 신어 봐도 돼요? 좀 끼면 한 치수 큰 거 볼게요.
My feet are a bit wide, so can I try them on? If they pinch I'll check a size up.
Real situation; 끼다 here = to feel tight
nuance: 신어 봐도 돼요? is the shoe-shop twin of 입어 봐도 돼요?: a customer asks a clerk to try footwear on. 신다 is the verb specifically for putting on shoes and socks (things on your feet), combined with -아 보다 'try' and -아도 돼요? 'may I?', so 'may I try putting them on?'. The body-part split is the whole point: 신다 for 신발 (shoes), 양말 (socks), 부츠; never 입다 for these. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 신어 봐도 될까요?, casual is 신어 봐도 돼?. Korean shoe sizes are stated in millimeters (250, 260, 270), unlike English/US numbers — a constant tourist surprise — so you'll pair this with a size like 250 사이즈로요. The nearest alternative is the generic 한번 봐도 돼요? (just to look); 신어 봐도 돼요? specifically means to put them on. The classic mistake is saying 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes because English uses one verb 'wear'; with shoes a native ear expects 신어. Spelling: 신어, from 신다 + 어 (not 신아).

입다 is for clothes on the body. Footwear uses 신다, so the shoe-shop phrase is 신어 봐도 돼요?

Korean shoes are sized in millimeters (250, 255, 260...). Say a mm number, e.g., 250 사이즈로요.
Writing 신아 봐도 돼요?
신다 + 어 = 신어 (the stem vowel ㅣ takes 어, not 아). Correct: 신어 봐도 돼요?

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar seller
Do you have it in black?
Naming the exact color you want
examples: 이거 다른 색 있어요?
Do you have this in another color?
Bare request holding one item
이 가방 다른 색 있어요? 흰색은 좀 부담스러워서요.
Do you have this bag in another color? White feels a bit much for me.
Giving a reason; 부담스럽다 = feels like too much
이 코트 마음에 드는데 다른 색 있어요? 네이비나 베이지요.
I like this coat — do you have other colors? Like navy or beige.
Real situation; 네이비/베이지 are common loan color words
nuance: 다른 색 있어요? is a customer asking a clerk whether an item comes in a different color; 다른 means 'other/different', 색 is the short spoken form of 색깔 ('color'), and 있어요? is 'is there / do you have?'. Politeness is everyday 해요체; casual is 다른 색 있어?, and a slightly softer poll is 다른 색깔도 있나요?. The verb of stock/availability in Korean is always 있다 ('to exist/have'), so 'do you have X?' becomes 'X 있어요?' — there is no separate verb 'to have' like English; this trips up beginners who hunt for a 'have' verb. The nearest alternative, 다른 거 있어요? ('do you have a different one?'), asks for a different item generally, while 다른 색 있어요? pins it to color specifically. Watch the word 다른 vs 다음 — 다른 = 'other', 다음 = 'next'; saying 다음 색 ('next color') is wrong. To name a color, use COLOR + 으로/로 있어요? (검은색으로 있어요?). English speakers also drop 색 and just say 다른 거, losing the color meaning.

Korean expresses 'have/there is' with 있다, not a possessive verb here. Ask 다른 색 있어요?

다른 색 = another color; 다음 색 = 'next color', which makes no sense in a shop. Use 다른.
Dropping 색 and asking only 다른 거 있어요?
That asks for a different item, not specifically a color. Keep 색: 다른 색 있어요?

english: Do you have a bigger one?
usage: Do you have a bigger one?
Polite size request to a clerk
Do you have a smaller one?
examples: 이거 더 큰 거 있어요?
Do you have this in a bigger one?
Bare size request holding an item
이 티셔츠 좀 작아요. 더 큰 거 있어요?
This T-shirt is a bit small. Do you have a bigger one?
Stating the problem then the request
허리가 좀 끼는데 더 큰 거 있어요? 한 치수 위로요.
It's a little tight at the waist — do you have a bigger size? One size up.
Real fitting situation; 치수 = clothing size
nuance: 더 큰 거 있어요? is a customer asking for a larger size or larger item; 더 means 'more', 큰 is the adjective 크다 ('big') in its noun-modifying form, 거 is the spoken 것 ('thing/one'), and 있어요? is 'do you have?'. So literally 'is there a more-big one?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 더 큰 거 있어?. The pair is 큰 거 (big one) vs 작은 거 (small one), and 더 큰/더 작은 for one step up or down; you can also ask 더 큰 사이즈 있어요? using the loanword 사이즈. The nearest alternative, 다른 사이즈 있어요? ('another size?'), is vaguer, while 더 큰 거 specifies the direction. usage: Softer, 중 = in the middle of, with -ㄴ가요
Using 할인 instead of the loanword 세일
examples: 이거 세일해요?
Is this on sale?
Bare question pointing at a tagged item
이거 세일해요? 얼마 할인되는 거예요?
Is this on sale? How much is the discount?
Following up on the amount; 할인되다 = be discounted
이 코너 전부 세일해요? 아니면 이것만요?
Is this whole section on sale, or just this one?
Real situation; 코너 = section, 이것만 = just this
nuance: 이거 세일해요? is a customer checking whether an item is discounted; 세일 is the English loanword 'sale' and 하다 makes it a verb, so 'does this do a sale / is this on sale?'. This is the everyday store word (department stores, franchises) — the opposite setting from 깎아 주세요 at a market. Politeness is 해요체; casual 세일해?, softer 세일 중인가요?. The native synonym is 할인 (割引, 'discount'): 할인해요? / 할인되는 거예요? mean the same and sound a touch more formal or written; the dividing line is register, not meaning — 세일 is breezy and spoken, 할인 is the word on signs and receipts. English speakers often say 온 세일 ('on sale') copying English, but Korean treats 세일 as a verb with 하다, so it's 세일해요?, not 온 세일이에요. Another error is confusing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (available to buy) — Korean 세일 only means discounted; 'is this for sale?' would be 이거 파는 거예요?.

세일 = discounted only. To ask if something is purchasable, say 이거 파는 거예요?, not 세일.

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar staff
examples: 이거 환불돼요?
Can I get a refund on this?
Bare question holding the item and receipt
사이즈가 안 맞아서요, 환불돼요?
It doesn't fit, so can I get a refund?
Giving the reason; 안 맞다 = doesn't fit
어제 샀는데 한 번도 안 썼어요. 영수증도 있고요. 환불돼요?
I bought it yesterday and never used it. I have the receipt too. Can I refund it?
Full real case; 한 번도 안 = not even once
nuance: 환불돼요? asks a clerk whether a refund (money back) is possible; 환불 is Sino-Korean 還拂 ('return-pay'), and 되다 here means 'to be possible/to work', so 'is a refund doable?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 환불돼?, more formal 환불 가능한가요?. The crucial contrast is 환불 (refund — money back) vs 교환 (exchange — swap for another item); Korean keeps these strictly separate, and English speakers who say 'return' blur them — decide whether you want your money (환불) or a different item (교환). You ask 환불돼요? to learn if it's allowed, and 환불해 주세요 to actually demand it. The spelling trap is 돼요 vs 되요: the polite form is 되 + 어 = 돼요, so 환불돼요, never 환불되요. Another trap is the loanword 리펀드 — nobody says it; the real word is 환불. Note Korea's culture: many shops require the receipt (영수증) and an unused tag, so pair this with 영수증 있어요.

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar staff
I'd like to exchange it for another
Stating what you want to swap to
examples: 이거 교환돼요?
Can I exchange this?
Bare question with item in hand
사이즈가 작아서요, 더 큰 걸로 교환돼요?
It's small, so can I exchange it for a bigger one?
Reason plus the swap; 걸로 = 것으로 (for the one)
색이 화면이랑 달라서요. 다른 색으로 교환돼요? 영수증 여기 있어요.
The color's different from the screen. Can I exchange it for another color? Here's the receipt.
Online-purchase return scene; 화면 = screen
nuance: 교환돼요? asks whether you can swap an item for a different size or color (or different item), said by a customer to a clerk; 교환 is Sino-Korean 交換 ('exchange/swap') and 되다 = 'to be possible', so 'is an exchange doable?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 교환돼?, formal 교환 가능한가요?. The defining contrast is again 교환 (swap item, no money returned) vs 환불 (money back); choose by what you want. To say what you're swapping to, use TARGET + 으로/로 교환: 다른 색으로 교환돼요?, 더 큰 걸로 교환돼요? — the particle 으로/로 ('into/for') is essential and English speakers often drop it. Spelling: 교환돼요, not 교환되요 (되+어=돼). usage: 반말 to a friend, rare to staff
Could you give me the receipt?
examples: 영수증 주세요.
Please give me the receipt.
Bare request as you pay
영수증 주세요. 혹시 교환할 수도 있어서요.
Please give me the receipt. In case I might exchange it.
Reason for keeping it; 혹시 = just in case
카드로 계산할게요. 영수증 주세요. 현금영수증도 해 주세요.
I'll pay by card. Please give me the receipt. And do a cash receipt too.
Real checkout; 현금영수증 = tax cash-receipt
nuance: 영수증 주세요 is a customer asking the cashier for the receipt; 영수증 is Sino-Korean 領收證 ('proof of receiving payment') and 주세요 is the polite 'please give (me)'. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 영수증 좀 주시겠어요?. In Korea the cashier often asks 영수증 드릴까요? ('shall I give you the receipt?') and many shops won't process a refund/exchange without it, so keeping it matters. Don't confuse 영수증 (paper receipt, proof of purchase) with 현금영수증 (a separate cash-receipt registered to your phone number for tax deduction) — Koreans are often asked 현금영수증 해 드릴까요?. A common English-speaker mistake is mispronouncing/misspelling it as 영수정 or 영수즁; it's 영수증. Also, 주세요 already means 'give me', so don't add 저에게 ('to me') — it's understood.

usage: Polite reply to a hovering clerk
examples: 그냥 둘러볼게요.
I'm just looking around.
Bare reply when a clerk asks if you need help
아, 괜찮아요. 그냥 둘러볼게요.
Oh, it's okay. I'm just browsing.
괜찮아요 softens the refusal of help
도움 필요하시면 부를게요. 일단 그냥 둘러볼게요.
I'll call you if I need help. For now I'm just looking.
Polite and friendly; 일단 = for now
nuance: 그냥 둘러볼게요 is what a customer says to a clerk who offers help, to signal 'no need, I'm just browsing'; 그냥 means 'just/for no particular reason', 둘러보다 is 'to look around', and -ㄹ게요 expresses the speaker's intention ('I'll...'). It politely declines assistance without buying pressure. Politeness is 해요체; casual 그냥 둘러볼게, and a very common equivalent is 구경 좀 할게요 (구경 = 'looking/browsing'). The phrase 둘러보다 (look around a space) vs 구경하다 (look at things for fun) overlap heavily here; both are natural, with 구경 sounding lighter. The nuance of -ㄹ게요 is 'I will (for my part)', which fits declining help; using the plain -아요 (둘러봐요) would sound like a statement of fact, not a polite intention, so the -ㄹ게요 ending is what makes it gracious. English speakers translate 'just looking' as 그냥 보고 있어요 ('I'm just watching'), which is understandable but flatter; the idiomatic brush-off is 그냥 둘러볼게요. Spelling: 둘러볼게요, pronounced with a tense 께, but written 게.

Spelling it 둘러볼께요.

usage: Same decision, asking to be handed it
examples: 이걸로 할게요.
I'll take this one.
Bare decision, pointing at your choice
고민했는데 이걸로 할게요. 계산해 주세요.
I thought about it — I'll take this one. Please ring it up.
고민하다 = to mull over; 계산 = checkout
둘 다 예쁜데 이걸로 할게요. 이거 하나만 주세요.
Both are pretty, but I'll take this one. Just this one, please.

nuance: 이걸로 할게요 is how a customer announces their final choice to buy; 이걸로 is 이것으로 ('with/by this one') contracted, and 하다 here means 'to go with / decide on', plus -ㄹ게요 'I'll', so 'I'll go with this one'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 이걸로 할게, formal 이걸로 하겠습니다. The particle 으로/로 ('with/by means of') is doing the selection work — Korean marks the chosen option with 으로/로, which is why it's 이걸로 (이것 + 으로), and English speakers who say 이거 할게요 (without 로) sound slightly off, though understandable. The near-twin 이걸로 주세요 ('give me this one') is interchangeable at checkout; 할게요 stresses your decision, 주세요 stresses the request to hand it over. The -ㄹ게요 ending again signals personal intention, perfect for committing to a purchase. A common mistake is using 이것을 할게요 (object particle 을) — selection takes 으로/로, not 을/를, so it's 이걸로. Spelling: 할게요, not 할께요.

english: Please wrap it up / pack it
examples: 이거 포장해 주세요.
Please wrap this up.

선물할 거라서요, 예쁘게 포장해 주세요.
It's a gift, so please wrap it nicely.
Reason plus 예쁘게 = prettily
따로따로 포장해 주세요. 선물할 거예요. 리본도 돼요?
Please wrap them separately. They're gifts. Can you add a ribbon too?
Detailed request; 따로따로 = separately

Politeness is 해요체; casual 포장해 줘, softer 포장 좀 해 주시겠어요?. Be careful: 포장 has a second meaning in restaurants — 'takeout/to go' (포장이요 = 'to take away'), the opposite of 먹고 갈게요 ('I'll eat here'). In a shop it means gift/parcel wrapping; for gifts specify 선물 포장 ('gift wrap'). The -아/어 주세요 pattern ('do X for me') is the workhorse request frame, and you stack adverbs before it: 예쁘게 포장해 주세요, 따로 포장해 주세요. English speakers literally translate 'wrap' as 싸다/싸 주세요 (싸다 = to wrap/bundle, also 'cheap' — confusing) which exists but sounds informal; the clean store word is 포장해 주세요. Another error is forgetting 주세요 and just saying 포장해요, which sounds like a statement, not a request.

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar vendor
Fuller, slightly more formal with 결제
examples: 카드 돼요?
Do you take card?
Bare question at a small stall before buying
카드 돼요? 아니면 현금만 받으세요?
Do you take card, or only cash?
Offering the alternative; 현금 = cash
카드 돼요? 만 원 이하도 카드 괜찮아요?
Do you take card? Is card okay even under 10,000 won?
Real small-shop worry; 이하 = or less
nuance: 카드 돼요? asks whether a shop accepts card payment, a real concern at markets, small stalls and food trucks where some are cash-only; 카드 is the loanword 'card' and 되다 means 'to work/be possible', so 'does card work (here)?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 카드 돼?, fuller 카드 결제 되나요? (결제 = 'payment/settlement'). The contrast set is 카드 (card) vs 현금 (cash); the flip question is 현금만 받아요? ('cash only?'). Spelling trap again: 돼요, not 되요 (되 + 어 = 돼). English speakers often build a long sentence like 신용카드를 받아요? ('do you receive credit card?') which is grammatical but stiff and over-literal; the idiomatic, native question is simply 카드 돼요?, using 되다 for 'is it possible'. Note that in Korea card is accepted almost everywhere by law for registered businesses, so this question mostly comes up for street vendors and very small operations.

되다's polite form is 돼요 (되+어). Ask 카드 돼요?

examples: 봉투 주세요.
Please give me a bag.
Bare request as items are rung up
봉투 주세요. 종이봉투로요.
A bag, please. A paper one.
Specifying type; 종이봉투 = paper bag
봉투 하나 주세요. 얼마예요? 비닐봉투는 돈 내야 하죠?

Real checkout; in Korea 비닐봉투 are paid
nuance: 봉투 주세요 asks the cashier for a bag, said by a customer; 봉투 means 'bag/envelope' (for shopping it's the carry bag) and 주세요 is 'please give me'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 봉투 줘, softer 봉투 하나 주시겠어요?. A key Korean reality: by law convenience stores and many shops charge for plastic bags (비닐봉투), so the cashier may ask 봉투 드릴까요? ('shall I give you a bag?') and you choose; paper bags are 종이봉투. Don't confuse 봉투 (bag/envelope) with 가방 (a proper bag/purse you own) — asking 가방 주세요 would mean 'give me a handbag'. The phrase pairs with type words: 비닐봉투 (plastic), 종이봉투 (paper). The flip is 봉투 필요 없어요 ('I don't need a bag'), increasingly common. English speakers may reach for 백 (bag) as a loanword, but for a shopping bag the word is 봉투; 백 sounds like a fashion bag. Also remember 주세요 already means 'give me', so no 저에게 needed.
